Group Exploratory Data Analysis: PBS Utah Major Donor Prediction

Authors

Erin Bednarik

Benjamin Hogan

Samantha Huang

Kate Klinger

Published

November 8, 2026

Introduction

Business Problem

Congress ended federal funding for public broadcasting in 2025, and PBS Utah now expects a recurring shortfall of about $2 million per year. Major donors, people who give $1,200 or more in a fiscal year, are a small share of donors but a large share of donor revenue. PBS Utah does not have a reliable, data-driven way to find which current non-major donors are most likely to become major donors, or at what giving level.

The project will produce a ranked prospect list that development staff can work through. A classification model will estimate each eligible donor’s probability of reaching $1,200 or more within 12 months (immediate priority) and within 3 to 5 years (long-term nurture), along with the most likely giving tier ($1,200, $2,000, or $5,000 and up). Major donor status is counted per person, except that a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200 counts as one major donor. Success will be judged by backtesting on earlier years, and the model has to beat a simple ranking by prior-year giving at a list of 1,000 donors, which is about what the officer cultivation program can work in a year. Results will be reported for all eligible donors and separately for donors who have never been major donors.

Target and Unit of Analysis

  • Unit of analysis: one person at the end of a fiscal year t (June 30), called a donor-year. A donor-year is eligible if the person gave in FY t and was not a major donor in FY t. Organizations are not units, and every feature uses only information dated on or before June 30 of FY t.
  • Target: whether the person becomes a major donor, meaning $1,200 or more of their own giving and soft credits in a fiscal year (or a couple reaching $1,200 together), in FY t+1 for the 12 month outcome, or in any year from FY t+1 to FY t+3 or FY t+5 for the longer outcomes.
  • Secondary target: the tier reached in the conversion year: $1,200, $2,000, or $5,000 and up.

How the EDA Changed the Framing

The business problem above is the revised version. The original statement was written before we looked at the data, and the EDA changed it in several ways. The final section lists every change with its evidence.

  • Major giving is rarer than the business case said: about 0.3% of donors and 8% of individual giving, not 1% and 19%.
  • Prior-year giving alone already ranks about 75% of next-year converters into a list of 1,000, so the original target of 25% of converters in the top 10% would not show that a model adds anything. The bar became the prior-year ranking at the list size officers can actually work.
  • About half of converters are former major donors, whom staff likely know already, so results are reported separately for never-major donors.
  • Too few donors reach $5,000 or more to support five tiers, so the tiers were reduced to three.
  • The University of Utah capacity fields turned out to encode PBS giving, so there is no outside capacity measure.
  • Officer contact changes the outcome, and the FY2026 influx changes the conversion rate, so both shaped the validation design.

Purpose of This Analysis

Each of the four team members completed an individual EDA. The four reached many of the same conclusions but used different definitions for who is eligible, how copy rows and legacy gifts are handled, and how models should be validated, so their headline numbers did not match. The team compared the four, agreed on one set of definitions, and this notebook applies them to the data in a single pass. It also brings in the strongest piece of each individual EDA:

  • Erin: donor-clustered bootstrap intervals, a lapsed-donor segment, giving-threshold rules as baselines, and legacy history indicators.
  • Benjamin: content-based cleaning rules, the decoding of the snapshot and University of Utah fields, and the checks on the FY2026 influx.
  • Kate: the master data dictionary and the split of the cultivation effect before and after program adoption.
  • Samantha: the time-aware eligibility rule, the rule that a response counts when it is dated, and the separation of raw and cleaned tables with an audit trail.

The individual EDAs remain available in each member’s repository, and the appendix describes each member’s contributions and the team’s use of AI tools. This notebook does not fit a model. It sets up the data, the target, the baselines, and the validation design that the modeling phase will use.

Agreed Decisions

The table summarizes the definitions used throughout this notebook. Each one is explained and checked in the section where it first matters.

Agreed decisions used throughout this notebook
# Topic Agreed rule
1 Copy rows Removed with content-based rules: a row with a broken link or a $0 amount that has an otherwise identical valid row. The copy labels in the row IDs are used only to check the rules.
2 Eligible population Donors who gave in fiscal year t and were not major that year. Lapsed donors, who gave in FY t-1 or FY t-2 but not FY t, are reported as a separate segment.
3 Former major donors Kept in the eligible population, flagged, and reported separately from never-major donors.
4 Legacy gifts Credited to the first listed person, with gifts listing a spouse flagged. Legacy history measures are kept alongside the amounts.
5 Snapshot years FY2021 to FY2025, with legacy giving history behind each snapshot.
6 Repeat solicitations Kept as repeat solicitations under the same marketing code.
7 Evidence for added signal A feature adds signal only if it separates converters within bands of prior-year giving.
8 Cultivation contact Contact flags are used in training only, and lists are scored with contact switched off. Results are also reported for donors who were not contacted. Operational and uplift models are out of scope.
9 Validation Rolling time-based tests on cohorts whose outcomes end before FY2026, with spouses in the same fold. The FY2025 cohort is used only for final training and reported once as a labeled check.
10 Baselines Prior-year giving (the bar to beat), with a “former major or $500” rule as a second check the model should also clear, officer selection measured on held-out donors, a three-part recency, frequency, and value score, and giving-threshold rules. Ties at the list cutoff are split evenly.
11 Uncertainty Donor-clustered bootstrap intervals for rates, recall, and lift.
12 Pipeline One shared Python build script, with the master data dictionary in the appendix.
13 Data-quality reporting Data issues are described where they affect the analysis.
14 Business problem statement The team’s revisions are summarized in the final section.
15 Household rule Major status is per person, but a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200 counts as one major donor. Both spouses are labeled as converted, and the couple is counted once.

Data Setup

This notebook combines the four individual EDAs into one analysis. All cleaning and panel construction happens in a single shared script, build_panel.py, so every section works from the same tables and the same definitions. The script applies the cleaning and eligibility rules the team agreed on, which are described in the sections that follow. On the first run it converts each raw CSV to a Parquet file in data_cache/, and later runs read the Parquet files.

from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from plotnine import *

import build_panel as bp

# the raw release sits one folder up; the cache lives next to this notebook
RAW = Path("../tables")
CACHE = Path("data_cache")

raw = bp.load_tables(RAW, CACHE)                 # raw tables, typed and snake-cased
clean, audit = bp.clean_tables(raw)              # shared cleaning rules
person_years = bp.build_person_years(clean)      # one row per person per fiscal year
cohorts = bp.build_cohorts(person_years)         # eligible and lapsed donors at each snapshot

# formatting helpers for inline numbers in the text
def n(x):
    return f"{x:,.0f}"

def pct(x, d=1):
    return f"{100 * x:.{d}f}%"

def pp(x, d=2):
    # a difference between two rates, in percentage points
    return f"{100 * x:.{d}f}"

def usd(x):
    return f"${x:,.0f}"

HEADER_NAMES = {"t": "FY t", "fy": "FY", "n_unique": "Distinct values", "dtype": "Type"}
HEADER_WORDS = (("_fy_t_", "_FY t_"), ("_fy26_", "_FY2026_"), ("_fy25_", "_FY2025_"), ("_fy2021_", "_FY2021_"),
                ("_fy_", "_FY_"), ("_ci_", "_CI_"), ("_uofu_", "_UofU_"), ("_pbs_", "_PBS_"), ("_rfv_", "_RFV_"))

def readable(col):
    # snake_case column name to a readable table header
    if col in HEADER_NAMES:
        return HEADER_NAMES[col]
    text = f"_{col}_"
    for old, new in HEADER_WORDS:
        text = text.replace(old, new)
    text = text.strip("_").replace("_", " ")
    return text[0].upper() + text[1:]

def show(df, pct_cols=(), pct_digits=1, caption=None):
    # render a polars frame as a captioned html table, keeping year columns free of separators
    out = df.with_columns([
        pl.col(c).map_elements(lambda v: f"{100 * v:.{pct_digits}f}%", return_dtype=pl.String) for c in pct_cols
    ])
    year_cols = ("fy", "fiscal_year", "first_fy", "last_fy", "t", "cohort", "last_cohort", "outcome_year")
    out = out.with_columns([pl.col(c).cast(pl.String) for c in out.columns if c in year_cols])
    out = out.rename({c: readable(c) for c in out.columns})
    styled = out.to_pandas().style.format(thousands=",", precision=2, na_rep="").hide(axis="index")
    return styled.set_caption(caption) if caption else styled

_ = theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(figure_size=(8, 4)))  # assign so the old theme is not printed

The shared build produces 572,487 person-years for 144,670 people and 2,209,529 cohort rows across all snapshots and outcome windows.

Data Sources and Cleaning

The Tables

The release has nine tables. Giving comes from three of them: Unite payments (FY2021 on), legacy Team Approach payments (before FY2021), and soft credits, which record gifts paid by donor-advised funds and other organizations on a person’s behalf. The other tables describe constituents, solicitations, Passport viewing, and the cultivation program.

# rows, columns, and fiscal-year coverage of each raw table
def fy_span(df, col, is_fy=False):
    years = df[col] if is_fy else df.select(bp.fiscal_year(col))[col]
    return f"FY{years.min()} to FY{years.max()}"

inventory = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "constituents_w_memberships", "rows": raw["constituents_w_memberships"].height, "one row per": "constituent", "coverage": "snapshot at end of FY2026"},
    {"table": "unite_payments", "rows": raw["unite_payments"].height, "one row per": "payment", "coverage": fy_span(raw["unite_payments"], "credit_date")},
    {"table": "team_approach_legacy_payments", "rows": raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].height, "one row per": "legacy gift", "coverage": fy_span(raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"], "gift_date")},
    {"table": "soft_credits", "rows": raw["soft_credits"].height, "one row per": "soft credit", "coverage": fy_span(raw["soft_credits"], "credit_date")},
    {"table": "campaign_codes", "rows": raw["campaign_codes"].height, "one row per": "marketing code", "coverage": "reference table"},
    {"table": "campaign_members", "rows": raw["campaign_members"].height, "one row per": "solicitation", "coverage": fy_span(raw["campaign_members"], "campaign_start_date")},
    {"table": "passport_viewing", "rows": raw["passport_viewing"].height, "one row per": "constituent, year, and genre", "coverage": fy_span(raw["passport_viewing"], "fiscal_year", True)},
    {"table": "cultivation", "rows": raw["cultivation"].height, "one row per": "selected donor and year", "coverage": fy_span(raw["cultivation"], "fiscal_year", True)},
    {"table": "officer_portfolios", "rows": raw["officer_portfolios"].height, "one row per": "officer portfolio", "coverage": "reference table"},
])
# legacy volume before FY1999, when the records become complete
legacy_fy_rows = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("gift_date")).agg(rows=pl.len())
legacy_pre99_max = legacy_fy_rows.filter(pl.col("fy") < 1999)["rows"].max()

show(inventory, caption="Raw tables in the release: size, unit, and years covered")

Legacy records technically start in FY1984, but no year before FY1999 has more than 176 gifts, so we treat FY1999 as the start of usable giving history. Solicitation and Passport data only begin in FY2021, which limits how far back the full set of features can reach.

Copy Rows

The known issues section of the student dictionary describes copy rows in the Unite payment, soft credit, and legacy tables: copies of other rows with one link removed or the amount set to $0, which are not part of anyone’s giving. Their IDs carry copy labels, but those labels are meant for checking cleaning rules, not for doing the cleaning. Our rule looks only at the content of each row. A row is a copy when it fails a validity check (a donor, recipient, or campaign code that does not link, an amount of $0 or less, or a legacy gift with no linked constituent) and an otherwise identical valid row exists, matching on every column except the row ID and the field that failed. Exact duplicate soft credits are removed first.

def check_summary(table, flags, df, row_id, amt):
    # rows failing each check, how many have a valid twin, and the dollars involved
    return (
        flags.join(df.select(row_id, amt), on=row_id)
        .group_by("check")
        .agg(rows_failing=pl.len(), with_valid_twin=pl.col("has_valid_twin").sum(), amount=pl.col(amt).sum())
        .with_columns(table=pl.lit(table))
        .select("table", "check", "rows_failing", "with_valid_twin", "amount")
    )

sc_dedup = raw["soft_credits"].unique(maintain_order=True)
legacy_unlinked = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].filter(pl.col("constituent_id_1").is_null())
copy_checks = pl.concat([
    check_summary("unite_payments", audit["pay_flags"], raw["unite_payments"], "payment_id", "payment_amount"),
    pl.DataFrame({"table": ["soft_credits"], "check": ["exact duplicate row"],
                  "rows_failing": [audit["sc_exact_duplicates"]], "with_valid_twin": [audit["sc_exact_duplicates"]],
                  "amount": [raw["soft_credits"]["credit_amount"].sum() - sc_dedup["credit_amount"].sum()]}),
    check_summary("soft_credits", audit["sc_flags"], sc_dedup, "credit_id", "credit_amount"),
    pl.DataFrame({"table": ["team_approach_legacy_payments"], "check": ["no linked constituent"],
                  "rows_failing": [audit["legacy_unlinked"]], "with_valid_twin": [audit["legacy_unlinked_copies"]],
                  "amount": [legacy_unlinked["payment_amount"].sum()]}),
], how="vertical_relaxed").sort("table", "check")

failing_without_twin = (copy_checks["rows_failing"] - copy_checks["with_valid_twin"]).sum()
pay_copy_amt = raw["unite_payments"].filter(pl.col("payment_id").is_in(audit["pay_copy_ids"].implode()))["payment_amount"].sum()

show(copy_checks, caption="Rows failing each validity check, and how many have an identical valid twin")
# compare the rows the rules removed with the copy labels
labels = bp.label_agreement(raw, audit)
label_mismatches = (labels["labeled_but_kept"] + labels["removed_but_unlabeled"]).sum()
show(labels, caption="Agreement between the content-based copy rules and the copy labels")

Every row that fails a check has a valid twin (none without one), so removing them drops no gift that is not already recorded. The rules remove 36,044 Unite payments worth $447,530, 192 soft credits, and 216,128 legacy rows. The second table shows that the rules and the labels agree exactly, with no mismatches. One individual EDA kept the 1,225 payments whose campaign code does not link, which counts those gifts twice, another very likely did, and a third removed copies by their labels, so this rule changes their cleaned tables slightly.

Organizations and Soft Credits

The constituent table includes organization records for the donor-advised fund and other sponsors that pay gifts on a person’s behalf. Their payments are the same money that the soft credits assign to people, so counting both would double count it. We identify the organizations by their constituent type and check that their payments match the soft credits.

orgs = bp.organization_ids(clean["constituents"])
org_fy = (
    clean["payments"].filter(pl.col("donor_id").is_in(orgs.implode()))
    .group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("credit_date"))
    .agg(org_payments=pl.len(), org_paid=pl.col("payment_amount").sum())
)
soft_fy = (
    clean["soft_credits"].group_by(fy=bp.fiscal_year("credit_date"))
    .agg(soft_credits=pl.len(), soft_credited=pl.col("credit_amount").sum())
)
org_vs_soft = org_fy.join(soft_fy, on="fy", how="full", coalesce=True).sort("fy")
max_gap = org_vs_soft.select((pl.col("org_paid") - pl.col("soft_credited")).abs().max()).item()

show(org_vs_soft, caption="Organization payments compared with soft credits by fiscal year")

There are 2 organization records, and their payments agree with the soft credits in every fiscal year (largest gap $0). A person’s fiscal-year giving is therefore their own positive payments plus their soft credits, with organization payments left out. Revenue totals do the reverse and count payments only.

Repeat Solicitations

cm = clean["campaign_members"]
cm_key = ["constituent_id", "marketing_code", "campaign_start_date"]
cm_exact_dups = cm.height - cm.n_unique()
cm_repeat = cm.filter(pl.struct(cm_key).is_duplicated())
cm_repeat_responses = int(cm_repeat["responded"].sum())

The solicitation table has 56,689 rows that exactly repeat another row, and 109,287 rows share a constituent, marketing code, and fiscal year with another row. None of those repeats is a response. The student dictionary says a constituent can be solicited more than once under the same code in a year when there is no response, and the table records no contact date that could tell the repeats apart, so we keep them as repeat solicitations. Solicitation adds little signal (see the solicitation section), so this choice has little effect.

Legacy Gifts

Legacy gifts were recorded by household in the old system, and a row can list more than one linked constituent.

legacy = clean["legacy"]
legacy_one_person = legacy["constituent_id_2"].is_null().mean()
legacy_spouse_rows = legacy["constituent_id_2"].is_not_null().sum()
legacy_spouse_share_amt = legacy.filter(pl.col("constituent_id_2").is_not_null())["payment_amount"].sum() / legacy["payment_amount"].sum()
legacy_max_ids = legacy.select(pl.sum_horizontal([pl.col(f"constituent_id_{i}").is_not_null() for i in range(1, 8)])).to_series().max()

After the copies are removed, 99.0% of linked legacy rows name a single person, and no row names more than 2. The 9,440 rows that list a spouse hold 0.88% of legacy dollars. We credit each legacy gift to the first listed person and flag the spouse rows, which keeps every gift counted once. Crediting both spouses would count those gifts twice, and dropping legacy amounts would lose the giving history that identifies returning major donors and makes the longer outcome windows testable. Legacy history measures such as years given and gift counts are added as features later.

Columns Not Used

def unused(name, df):
    # columns that are completely blank or hold a single value
    out = []
    for c in df.columns:
        vals = df[c].drop_nulls()
        if df[c].dtype == pl.String:
            vals = vals.filter(vals != "")
        if vals.n_unique() <= 1:
            out.append({"table": name, "column": c, "status": "blank" if vals.len() == 0 else "single value"})
    return out

unused_cols = pl.DataFrame([row for name, df in raw.items() for row in unused(name, df)])
unused_by_table = unused_cols.group_by("table").agg(columns=pl.len()).sort(["columns", "table"], descending=[True, False])
total_cols = sum(df.width for df in raw.values())
show(unused_by_table, caption="Columns that are blank or hold a single value, by table")

61 of the 129 columns are blank or hold a single value, most of them masked fields in the legacy and campaign code tables. Because they do not vary, they cannot help a model and are not used as features. Portfolio capacity is the one exception worth keeping: it is 125 for every portfolio, but it sets the realistic list size of 1,000 donors a year. A few columns that do vary are also left out because they repeat other columns or leak future information; those are covered in the snapshot fields section, and the master data dictionary in the appendix lists the status of every column.

Missing Values

The columns that are completely blank are covered above. The table below covers the partly missing fields that matter for the analysis, plus two values that act as missing (“Unknown” gender and a year with no Passport record). For each one it gives how much is missing, why, and what we do about it.

con_raw = raw["constituents_w_memberships"]
people_raw = con_raw.filter(pl.col("primary_constituent_type") != "Organization")
legacy_raw = raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"]
cm_raw = raw["campaign_members"]
blank_age_orgs = con_raw.filter(pl.col("age").is_null())["primary_constituent_type"].eq("Organization").all()
marital_matches_spouse = (con_raw["marital_status"].is_null() == con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"].is_null()).all()

# eligible donor-years (FY2021 to FY2025) with no Passport record in FY t
elig_recent = cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "active") & (pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
pv_years = raw["passport_viewing"].select("constituent_id", t=pl.col("fiscal_year")).unique()
no_passport = elig_recent.join(pv_years, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="anti").height / elig_recent.height

def share_missing(s):
    return s.is_null().mean()

def count_missing(s):
    return int(s.is_null().sum())

missing = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Spouse Constituent ID", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["spouse_constituent_id"]),
     "why": "No spouse on file", "handling": "Treated as single: own couple ID, no household combination"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Marital Status", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["marital_status"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["marital_status"]),
     "why": "Blank exactly when no spouse is on file" if marital_matches_spouse else "Mostly when no spouse is on file",
     "handling": "Dropped; repeats spouse on file"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Gender = Unknown", "missing": (people_raw["gender"] == "Unknown").mean(), "rows": int((people_raw["gender"] == "Unknown").sum()),
     "why": "Not recorded; may mark thinner records", "handling": "Kept as its own level"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Age, gender, giving group", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["age"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["age"]),
     "why": "Blank only for the two organization records" if blank_age_orgs else "Mixed",
     "handling": "Organizations are not units of analysis"},
    {"table": "constituents", "field": "Major Donor Class", "missing": share_missing(con_raw["major_donor_class_pbs_utah"]), "rows": count_missing(con_raw["major_donor_class_pbs_utah"]),
     "why": "Blank means never a major donor", "handling": "Dropped; describes FY2026 giving"},
    {"table": "legacy payments", "field": "constituent_id_1", "missing": share_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_1"]), "rows": count_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_1"]),
     "why": "Copy rows with the link removed", "handling": "Removed by the copy rule"},
    {"table": "legacy payments", "field": "constituent_id_2", "missing": share_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_2"]), "rows": count_missing(legacy_raw["constituent_id_2"]),
     "why": "Gift lists one person", "handling": "Gift credited to the first person; spouse rows flagged"},
    {"table": "campaign members", "field": "responded_date, response_type", "missing": share_missing(cm_raw["responded_date"]), "rows": count_missing(cm_raw["responded_date"]),
     "why": "No response to that solicitation", "handling": "Structural, not imputed; responses counted by response date"},
    {"table": "passport viewing", "field": "No record in FY t (eligible donor-years)", "missing": no_passport, "rows": round(no_passport * elig_recent.height),
     "why": "No linked account, no consent, or no viewing; the data cannot tell which", "handling": "Own \"no viewing record\" level, never set to zero viewing"},
    {"table": "officer portfolios", "field": "rollout_fy", "missing": share_missing(raw["officer_portfolios"]["rollout_fy"]), "rows": count_missing(raw["officer_portfolios"]["rollout_fy"]),
     "why": "The one portfolio that never adopted the program", "handling": "Treated as not adopted"},
])
payment_nulls = sum(raw[t][c].null_count() for t in ("unite_payments", "soft_credits") for c in raw[t].columns)
show(missing.select("table", "field", "rows", "missing", "why", "handling"), pct_cols=["missing"], caption="Partly missing fields that matter: how much, why, and how they are handled")

Most of the missing values are structural rather than lost data: a blank spouse means no spouse, a blank response date means no response, and a blank major donor class means never major. None of the fields that feed the model is imputed. Two cases need care in modeling. Unknown gender covers about a fifth of people and is kept as its own level, since it may say more about how complete a record is than about the person. A missing Passport year is the more serious gap, because about half of eligible donor-years have no viewing record and the data cannot say why, so any Passport feature carries its own “no viewing record” level. The payment and soft credit tables have no missing values in the fields we use.

Cleaned Tables

cleaned = pl.DataFrame([
    {"table": "unite_payments", "raw_rows": raw["unite_payments"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["payments"].height},
    {"table": "soft_credits", "raw_rows": raw["soft_credits"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["soft_credits"].height},
    {"table": "team_approach_legacy_payments", "raw_rows": raw["team_approach_legacy_payments"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["legacy"].height},
    {"table": "campaign_members", "raw_rows": raw["campaign_members"].height, "cleaned_rows": clean["campaign_members"].height},
]).with_columns(rows_removed=pl.col("raw_rows") - pl.col("cleaned_rows"))
show(cleaned, caption="Rows before and after cleaning")

The raw tables are kept unchanged and the cleaned versions are built from them, so every removal can be traced back to the rule that caused it.

Giving Panel and Eligible Population

Fiscal-Year Giving

The panel has one row per person per fiscal year in which they gave. A person’s giving in a year is the sum of their own Unite payments, their soft credits, and the legacy gifts credited to them, with organization payments left out. Each row also keeps the pieces of that total (recurring and one-time payments, soft credits, legacy amounts, and the share of legacy dollars from gifts that list a spouse), which later sections use as features.

# where each fiscal year's individual giving comes from
source_mix = (
    person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 1999)
    .with_columns(era=pl.when(pl.col("fy") >= 2021).then(pl.lit("FY2021 to FY2026 (Unite)")).otherwise(pl.lit("FY1999 to FY2020 (legacy)")))
    .group_by("era")
    .agg(person_years=pl.len(), people=pl.col("constituent_id").n_unique(),
         unite=pl.col("unite_amt").sum(), soft_credits=pl.col("soft_amt").sum(), legacy=pl.col("legacy_amt").sum())
    .sort("era", descending=True)
)

# donors who give again the next year, around the switch from legacy to Unite
donor_years = person_years.select("constituent_id", "fy")
def retention(fy):
    this_year = donor_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy)
    return this_year.join(donor_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy + 1), on="constituent_id", how="semi").height / this_year.height
ret_19, ret_20, ret_21 = retention(2019), retention(2020), retention(2021)

show(source_mix, caption="Where individual giving comes from in the legacy and Unite eras")

From FY2021 on, individual giving comes from Unite payments and soft credits, and before that from legacy gifts. The switch between the two systems does not break donors’ histories: the share of donors who give again the next year moves smoothly from 72.5% (FY2019 to FY2020) to 74.7% (FY2020 to FY2021) and 75.1% (FY2021 to FY2022). Legacy history can therefore sit behind each Unite-era snapshot.

The Household Rule

Major status is counted per person, except that a couple whose combined giving reaches $1,200, when neither spouse does alone, counts as one major donor. Both spouses are labeled as major in that year and share a couple ID, so the couple can be counted once.

recent_py = person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
combined_only_rows = person_years.filter("major_combined_only")
combined_only_couple_years = combined_only_rows.select("couple_id", "fy").unique().height

majors_by_fy = (
    recent_py.filter(pl.col("major"))
    .group_by("fy")
    .agg(people_major=pl.len(), major_units=pl.col("couple_id").n_unique(),
         combined_only=pl.col("major_combined_only").sum())
    .sort("fy")
)
both_individually_major = (
    recent_py.filter(pl.col("major_individual") & pl.col("spouse_id").is_not_null())
    .join(recent_py.filter("major_individual").select(spouse_id=pl.col("constituent_id"), fy="fy"),
          on=["spouse_id", "fy"], how="semi")
    .height
)
show(majors_by_fy, caption="Major donors per year, with couples counted once")

In the whole panel, 1 couple-year reaches $1,200 only in combination (2 people, in FY2026), and no couples have both spouses major on their own in the same year. The rule therefore changes the count of major donors by one unit, so it matters for correctness more than for the numbers in this data. The major_units column counts each couple once, which is the count used for donor shares.

Eligible Population

At the end of each fiscal year t, the eligible population is every donor who gave that year and was not a major donor that year. Donors who gave in FY t-1 or FY t-2 but not in FY t form a separate lapsed segment. Within both groups, donors who were major in any earlier year, including the legacy years, are flagged as former major donors. A donor converts when they become major (under the household rule) in the outcome window.

c12 = cohorts.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
eligible_summary = (
    c12.group_by("t", "segment")
    .agg(donors=pl.len(), former_majors=pl.col("former_major").sum(), converters=pl.col("converted").sum(),
         in_validation=pl.col("in_validation").first())
    .with_columns(rate=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("donors"))
    .sort("segment", "t")
)
seg = {s: c12.filter(pl.col("segment") == s) for s in ("active", "lapsed")}
active_conv = seg["active"]["converted"].sum()
lapsed_conv = seg["lapsed"]["converted"].sum()
active_val = seg["active"].filter("in_validation")
show(eligible_summary, pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Eligible donors and 12 month converters by cohort and segment")

From FY2021 to FY2025 there are about 32,000 eligible donors a year and 270 12 month converters in total. The lapsed segment adds about 14,000 donors a year but only 9 converters, which supports keeping it separate: lapsed donors rarely come back as major donors within a year, and mixing them in would dilute the eligible group. Following the validation decision, only the FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts (189 active converters) are used to compare models. The FY2025 cohort, whose outcomes fall in FY2026, is used only in final training.

Reconciling the Four Individual EDAs

The individual EDAs reported different converter counts because they used different eligibility rules and, in one case, different years. Rebuilding each definition from the shared panel shows that the counts all come from the same data.

py_major = person_years.select("constituent_id", "fy", "total", "major_individual")
first_fy = person_years.group_by("constituent_id").agg(first_fy=pl.col("fy").min())

def ids(df):
    return df["constituent_id"].unique().implode()

def converters(eligible, t):
    # individual-rule converters: major on their own in FY t+1
    nxt = py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t + 1) & pl.col("major_individual"))
    return eligible.filter(pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(ids(nxt))).height

def count(years, rule):
    total = 0
    for t in years:
        major_t = ids(py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t) & pl.col("major_individual")))
        gave_t = py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") == t) & ~pl.col("major_individual")).select("constituent_id")
        if rule == "gave in FY t":
            elig = gave_t
        elif rule == "ever gave by FY t":
            elig = first_fy.filter((pl.col("first_fy") <= t) & ~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(major_t)).select("constituent_id")
        elif rule == "gave in FY t, not major since FY2021":
            since21 = ids(py_major.filter(pl.col("fy").is_between(2021, t - 1) & pl.col("major_individual")))
            elig = gave_t.filter(~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(since21))
        elif rule == "gave in FY t, never major":
            ever = ids(py_major.filter((pl.col("fy") < t) & pl.col("major_individual")))
            elig = gave_t.filter(~pl.col("constituent_id").is_in(ever))
        total += converters(elig, t)
    return total

reconciliation = pl.DataFrame([
    {"definition": "Agreed: gave in FY t, household rule", "used_by": "this notebook", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": active_conv},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, per person only", "used_by": "Benjamin, Kate", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2021, 2026), "gave in FY t")},
    {"definition": "Ever gave by FY t, per person only", "used_by": "Samantha", "cohorts": "FY2021 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2021, 2026), "ever gave by FY t")},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, not major since FY2021", "used_by": "Erin (active donors)", "cohorts": "FY2023 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2023, 2026), "gave in FY t, not major since FY2021")},
    {"definition": "Gave in FY t, never major in any year", "used_by": "reference", "cohorts": "FY2023 to FY2025", "converters_12m": count(range(2023, 2026), "gave in FY t, never major")},
])
rc = {r["used_by"]: r["converters_12m"] for r in reconciliation.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(reconciliation, caption="Each individual EDA's converter count rebuilt from the shared panel")

Each individual EDA’s count is reproduced exactly from the shared panel:

  • Benjamin’s and Kate’s 269 converters are the agreed definition without the household rule. The household rule adds 1.
  • Samantha’s 293 include everyone who had ever given, so they add 24 lapsed donors of any length to Benjamin’s and Kate’s count.
  • Erin’s 99 active converters come from three cohorts and exclude anyone major since FY2021. Of these, 19 had been major before FY2021, which only shows up when legacy amounts are used. Erin’s two lapsed converters come from her own lapsed definition, which is not rebuilt here.

The agreed definition keeps the full giving history (legacy amounts back to FY1999), all five Unite-era cohorts, and former major donors as a flagged group. Samantha’s broader rule finds a few more converters, but it does so by adding tens of thousands of long-lapsed donors who almost never convert. Keeping recent lapsed donors as a separate segment captures some of those converters without diluting the main group.

How Rare Major Giving Is

Major Donors as a Share of Donors and Revenue

The business case describes major donors as about 1% of the donor file and about 19% of donor revenue. The table checks this for each fiscal year from FY2021 on. Donors are people who gave that year. Major donors are counted in units, so a couple that qualifies only in combination counts once, and revenue is individual giving.

share_by_fy = (
    person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
    .group_by("fy")
    .agg(
        donors=pl.len(),
        major_donors=pl.col("couple_id").filter(pl.col("major")).n_unique(),
        revenue=pl.col("total").sum(),
        major_revenue=pl.col("total").filter(pl.col("major")).sum(),
    )
    .with_columns(share_of_donors=pl.col("major_donors") / pl.col("donors"),
                  share_of_revenue=pl.col("major_revenue") / pl.col("revenue"))
    .sort("fy")
)
pooled_share = share_by_fy.select(
    donors=pl.col("major_donors").sum() / pl.col("donors").sum(),
    revenue=pl.col("major_revenue").sum() / pl.col("revenue").sum(),
).row(0, named=True)

show(share_by_fy, pct_cols=["share_of_donors", "share_of_revenue"], pct_digits=2, caption="Major donors as a share of donors and of individual giving")

Major donors are 0.25% to 0.38% of donors each year (0.32% pooled) and give 5.2% to 10.7% of revenue (7.8% pooled), well below the 1% and 19% in the business case. Benjamin’s and Kate’s EDAs, the two that checked these figures, found the same gap, and none of the alternative definitions they tried (a $1,000 threshold, combining spouses) closes it. The team’s revised problem statement restates these figures from the data.

Giving Around the $1,200 Line

If many donors gave just below $1,200, crossing the line would be a small step and easy to predict. The bands below show annual giving per person-year from FY2021 on.

edges = [250, 500, 750, 1000, 1200, 1200.01, 2000, 2000.01, 5000, 5000.01]
band_labels = ["under $250", "$250 to $499", "$500 to $749", "$750 to $999", "$1,000 to $1,199", "exactly $1,200",
               "$1,200.01 to $1,999", "exactly $2,000", "$2,000.01 to $4,999", "exactly $5,000", "over $5,000"]
recent = person_years.filter(pl.col("fy") >= 2021)
bands = (
    recent.with_columns(band=pl.col("total").cut(edges, labels=band_labels, left_closed=True).cast(pl.Enum(band_labels)))
    .group_by("band").agg(person_years=pl.len())
)
# show every band, including empty ones, in order
bands = (
    pl.DataFrame({"band": band_labels}).with_columns(pl.col("band").cast(pl.Enum(band_labels)))
    .join(bands, on="band", how="left").with_columns(pl.col("person_years").fill_null(0))
)
recent_majors = recent.filter("major_individual")
exact_tier_share = recent_majors["total"].is_in([1200, 2000, 5000, 10000]).mean()
nonmajor_max = recent.filter(~pl.col("major_individual"))["total"].max()
just_under = recent.filter(pl.col("total").is_between(750, 1200, closed="left")).height
between_tiers = recent.filter((pl.col("total") > 1200) & (pl.col("total") < 2000)).height
at_600 = recent.filter(pl.col("total").is_between(500, 750)).select((pl.col("total") == 600).mean()).item()

show(bands, caption="Person-years by band of annual giving, FY2021 to FY2026")

Giving is not smooth around the line. No non-major donor-year exceeds $1,100, only 2 fall between $750 and $1,199, and none fall strictly between $1,200 and $2,000. 89.9% of major donor-years are exactly $1,200, $2,000, $5,000, or $10,000, and 96.9% of donor-years in the $500 to $749 band are exactly $600. Becoming a major donor is therefore a jump from the regular giving range, not a small step over the line. As later sections show, the donors who make that jump still come mostly from the top of the regular range.

Conversion Base Rates

The rates below use the eligible population from the previous section. Intervals come from a donor-clustered bootstrap: each resample draws whole couples (or single donors) with replacement, keeping all of their cohort rows together, so repeated appearances of the same donor do not make the estimate look more certain than it is.

import numpy as np

def clustered_rate(df, reps=1000, seed=20261009):
    # point estimate and 95% interval, resampling couple_id clusters with replacement
    # sort so the same seed always draws the same couples
    g = df.group_by("couple_id").agg(rows=pl.len(), conv=pl.col("converted").sum()).sort("couple_id")
    rows, conv = g["rows"].to_numpy(), g["conv"].to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = len(g)
    draws = np.empty(reps)
    for r in range(reps):
        pick = rng.integers(0, m, m)
        draws[r] = conv[pick].sum() / rows[pick].sum()
    return conv.sum() / rows.sum(), np.quantile(draws, 0.025), np.quantile(draws, 0.975)

active = cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "active") & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))
specs = [
    ("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 1)),
    ("12 months", "never major", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & ~pl.col("former_major"))),
    ("12 months", "former major", "FY2021 to FY2025", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("former_major"))),
    ("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2024 (validation)", active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("in_validation"))),
    ("12 months", "lapsed segment", "FY2021 to FY2025", cohorts.filter((pl.col("segment") == "lapsed") & (pl.col("window") == 1) & (pl.col("t") >= 2021))),
    ("within 3 years", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2023", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 3)),
    ("within 5 years", "all eligible", "FY2021", active.filter(pl.col("window") == 5)),
]
rate_rows = []
for outcome, group, cohorts_used, df in specs:
    est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(df)
    rate_rows.append({"outcome": outcome, "group": group, "cohorts": cohorts_used, "donor_years": df.height,
                      "converters": int(df["converted"].sum()), "rate": est, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi})
base_rates = pl.DataFrame(rate_rows)
br = {(r["outcome"], r["group"], r["cohorts"]): r for r in base_rates.iter_rows(named=True)}
r12 = br[("12 months", "all eligible", "FY2021 to FY2025")]
r12_never = br[("12 months", "never major", "FY2021 to FY2025")]
r12_former = br[("12 months", "former major", "FY2021 to FY2025")]

show(base_rates, pct_cols=["rate", "ci_low", "ci_high"], pct_digits=3, caption="Conversion base rates with couple-clustered 95% intervals")

Conversion is rare. 0.17% of eligible donors become major donors the next year (95% interval 0.15% to 0.19%), about 54 people a year. Former major donors convert at 14.5%, compared with 0.083% for never-major donors, and they account for 51% of converters while being 0.6% of eligible donors. This is why results must be reported separately for never-major donors: staff likely already know their lapsed major donors, and a list that mostly finds them would look strong without adding much. The intervals are narrowest for the pooled 12 month rate and widest for the lapsed segment, which rests on only 9 converters. The 5 year rate comes from a single cohort, so its interval reflects donor variation within that cohort but not variation between years.

Tiers Reached at Conversion

# tier in the conversion year, using the couple's combined giving when only the couple qualifies
tier_basis = person_years.with_columns(
    tier_total=pl.when(pl.col("major_combined_only")).then(pl.col("total") + pl.col("spouse_total")).otherwise(pl.col("total"))
).with_columns(conv_tier=pl.col("tier_total").cut(bp.TIERS, labels=bp.TIER_LABELS, left_closed=True).cast(pl.Enum(bp.TIER_LABELS)))

conv_tiers = (
    active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("converted"))
    .select("constituent_id", fy=pl.col("t") + 1)
    .join(tier_basis.select("constituent_id", "fy", "conv_tier"), on=["constituent_id", "fy"])
    .group_by("conv_tier").agg(converters=pl.len())
    .with_columns(share=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("converters").sum())
    .sort("conv_tier")
)
tier_n = {str(r["conv_tier"]): r["converters"] for r in conv_tiers.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(conv_tiers, pct_cols=["share"], caption="Tier reached by 12 month converters")

Of the 270 12 month converters, 158 reach the $1,200 tier, 99 reach $2,000, and only 13 reach $5,000 or more. This supports the agreed three-tier scheme, and it means the tier model is mostly a choice between $1,200 and $2,000, with too few cases above that to model separately.

Summary for Modeling

  • The 12 month conversion rate is about 0.17%, so models should be judged on ranking measures at a fixed list size, not accuracy.
  • Former major donors are a small, high-converting group and are reported separately.
  • Major giving is a jump to a tier amount, so the model has to find donors who are likely to make that jump, not donors who are close to the line.
  • Single-cohort results are noisy, and clustered intervals should accompany every rate, recall, and lift reported in modeling.

Signals From Giving History

This section asks which parts of a donor’s giving history add information beyond how much they gave in FY t. Every feature is measured at the end of FY t from gifts dated on or before June 30 of that year, so nothing comes from the outcome years. Choosing features is part of model selection, so the section uses only the validation cohorts (FY2021 to FY2024) and leaves out the FY2025 cohort. The main outcome is the 12 month window, with a 3 year check at the end. The lapsed segment is left out because it has too few converters to compare features.

gifts = bp.individual_gifts(clean)
PRIOR_BANDS = ["$60 or less", "$61 to $120", "$121 to $240", "$241 to $500", "over $500"]

def with_features(rows):
    # giving-history features at the end of FY t plus the prior-year giving band
    return rows.join(bp.giving_features(rows, person_years, gifts), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left").with_columns(
        band=pl.col("prior_total").cut([60, 120, 240, 500], labels=PRIOR_BANDS).cast(pl.Enum(PRIOR_BANDS))
    )

feat12 = with_features(active.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("in_validation")))
feat3 = with_features(active.filter((pl.col("window") == 3) & pl.col("in_validation")))
base12 = feat12["converted"].mean()

Prior-Year Giving

band_rows = []
for b in PRIOR_BANDS:
    d = feat12.filter(pl.col("band") == b)
    est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(d)
    band_rows.append({"prior_year_giving": b, "donor_years": d.height, "converters": int(d["converted"].sum()),
                      "rate": est, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi,
                      "never_major_rate": d.filter(~pl.col("former_major"))["converted"].mean()})
prior_bands = pl.DataFrame(band_rows).with_columns(
    share_of_donors=pl.col("donor_years") / pl.col("donor_years").sum(),
    share_of_converters=pl.col("converters") / pl.col("converters").sum(),
)
pb = {r["prior_year_giving"]: r for r in prior_bands.iter_rows(named=True)}
low_bands = prior_bands.filter(pl.col("prior_year_giving").is_in(PRIOR_BANDS[:3])).select(
    pl.col("share_of_donors", "share_of_converters").sum()).row(0, named=True)

show(prior_bands, pct_cols=["rate", "ci_low", "ci_high", "never_major_rate", "share_of_donors", "share_of_converters"], pct_digits=2, caption="12 month conversion by prior-year giving band, FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts")
import pandas as pd

def percent_labels(breaks):
    return [f"{100 * b:.0f}%" for b in breaks]

band_plot = []
for b in PRIOR_BANDS:
    d = feat12.filter(pl.col("band") == b)
    for group, dd in [("All eligible", d), ("Never major", d.filter(~pl.col("former_major")))]:
        est, lo, hi = clustered_rate(dd)
        band_plot.append({"band": b.replace("$", r"\$"), "group": group, "rate": est, "lo": lo, "hi": hi})
band_pd = pl.DataFrame(band_plot).to_pandas()
band_pd["band"] = pd.Categorical(band_pd["band"], categories=[b.replace("$", r"\$") for b in PRIOR_BANDS], ordered=True)

(
    ggplot(band_pd, aes("band", "rate", fill="group"))
    + geom_col(position=position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.75)
    + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin="lo", ymax="hi"), position=position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.25)
    + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent_labels)
    + labs(x="Giving in FY t", y="Converted in FY t+1", fill="",
           title="12 month conversion rises steeply with prior-year giving",
           subtitle="FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts, 95% couple-clustered intervals")
    + theme(legend_position="top")
)

Conversion rises steeply with prior-year giving. Donors who gave more than $500 in FY t convert at 11.5% and supply 67.7% of converters while making up 0.87% of eligible donor-years. Donors who gave $240 or less are 93.2% of donor-years and supply only 13.2% of converters. The pattern holds for never-major donors, whose top-band rate is 5.0%. Distance to $1,200 ranks donors in exactly the same order as prior-year giving, so it is not treated as a separate feature.

These five bands are the bands used for every comparison in the rest of this section.

Features at the Prediction Date

The shared build adds the following features for each eligible donor at the end of FY t. The three-year total suggested in the individual EDAs is split into prior-year giving and giving in the two years before, since prior-year giving is already held constant by the bands.

Giving-history features built for each donor-year
Feature Definition
Former major donor Major in any earlier fiscal year, including legacy years
Years given, last 5 Fiscal years with a gift from FY t-4 to FY t
Years since first gift Years from the first fiscal year with a gift, including legacy years, to FY t
Legacy-era giving years Fiscal years with a legacy gift, Erin’s legacy history indicator
Change from last year FY t giving compared with FY t-1 giving
Giving in the two years before Total giving in FY t-2 and FY t-1
Largest gift share of FY t Largest single gift as a share of FY t giving
Largest gift in FY t Largest single gift in FY t
Upgrade or additional gift in FY t A Unite payment in FY t with that gift type
Soft credit before FY t, in FY t At least one soft credit in an earlier year, or in FY t
Monthly sustainer amount Recurring payments in FY t divided by their number
Days since last gift Days from the last gift to June 30 of FY t

Signals Within Giving Bands

Following decision 7, a feature adds signal only if it separates converters among donors who gave about the same amount. For each level of a feature, we count how many converters we would expect if those donors converted at the average rate of their prior-year band, and divide the observed converters by that number. A ratio above 1 means the level converts more often than its prior-year giving predicts. A ratio near 1 means the feature’s overall lift is prior-year giving in another form. Intervals come from the couple-clustered bootstrap used for the base rates. The same ratio is computed for never-major donors using their own band rates. The overall lift, the level’s rate divided by the base rate of 0.148%, is shown for context.

def yes_no(col):
    return pl.when(pl.col(col)).then(pl.lit("yes")).otherwise(pl.lit("no"))

# (feature, level expression, levels in display order)
signal_specs = [
    ("Former major donor", yes_no("former_major"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Years given, last 5", pl.col("years_last5").cast(pl.String) + " of 5", ["1 of 5", "2 of 5", "3 of 5", "4 of 5", "5 of 5"]),
    ("Years since first gift", pl.col("years_since_first_gift").cut([1, 3, 10], labels=["1", "2 to 3", "4 to 10", "over 10"]).cast(pl.String),
     ["1", "2 to 3", "4 to 10", "over 10"]),
    ("Legacy-era giving years", pl.when(pl.col("legacy_years") == 0).then(pl.lit("none"))
        .when(pl.col("legacy_years") <= 4).then(pl.lit("1 to 4")).otherwise(pl.lit("5 or more")), ["none", "1 to 4", "5 or more"]),
    ("Change from last year", pl.when(pl.col("prev_total") == 0).then(pl.lit("no gift last year"))
        .when(pl.col("prior_total") > pl.col("prev_total")).then(pl.lit("gave more"))
        .when(pl.col("prior_total") < pl.col("prev_total")).then(pl.lit("gave less")).otherwise(pl.lit("gave the same")),
     ["no gift last year", "gave less", "gave the same", "gave more"]),
    ("Giving in the two years before", pl.when(pl.col("two_years_before") == 0).then(pl.lit("$0"))
        .when(pl.col("two_years_before") <= 500).then(pl.lit("$1 to $500"))
        .when(pl.col("two_years_before") < 1200).then(pl.lit("$501 to $1,199")).otherwise(pl.lit("$1,200 or more")),
     ["$0", "$1 to $500", "$501 to $1,199", "$1,200 or more"]),
    ("Largest gift share of FY t", pl.when(pl.col("largest_gift_t") >= pl.col("prior_total")).then(pl.lit("all in one gift"))
        .when(pl.col("largest_gift_t") >= 0.5 * pl.col("prior_total")).then(pl.lit("half or more")).otherwise(pl.lit("under half")),
     ["under half", "half or more", "all in one gift"]),
    ("Largest gift in FY t", pl.col("largest_gift_t").cut([100, 250, 500], labels=["$100 or less", "$101 to $250", "$251 to $500", "over $500"]).cast(pl.String),
     ["$100 or less", "$101 to $250", "$251 to $500", "over $500"]),
    ("Upgrade gift in FY t", yes_no("upgrade_gift"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Additional gift in FY t", yes_no("additional_gift"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Soft credit before FY t", yes_no("soft_before"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Soft credit in FY t", yes_no("soft_in_t"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Monthly sustainer amount", pl.when(~pl.col("sustainer")).then(pl.lit("not a sustainer"))
        .when(pl.col("monthly_amount") <= 10).then(pl.lit("$10 or less"))
        .when(pl.col("monthly_amount") <= 25).then(pl.lit("$11 to $25")).otherwise(pl.lit("over $25")),
     ["not a sustainer", "$10 or less", "$11 to $25", "over $25"]),
    ("Days since last gift", pl.col("days_since_last_gift").cut([30, 90, 180], labels=["30 or less", "31 to 90", "91 to 180", "over 180"]).cast(pl.String),
     ["30 or less", "31 to 90", "91 to 180", "over 180"]),
]

def couple_draws(df, reps=1000, seed=20261009):
    # each bootstrap draw counts how many times every couple is picked
    couples = df["couple_id"].unique().sort()
    idx = couples.search_sorted(df["couple_id"]).to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = len(couples)
    w = np.stack([np.bincount(rng.integers(0, m, m), minlength=m) for _ in range(reps)]).astype(np.float32)
    return idx, w

def within_band_ratio(df, idx, w, levels):
    # observed converters over the number expected from each level's mix of prior-year bands
    nb, nl = len(PRIOR_BANDS), len(levels)
    level_i = df["level"].replace_strict({lev: i for i, lev in enumerate(levels)}, return_dtype=pl.Int64).to_numpy()
    cell = df["band"].to_physical().to_numpy() * nl + level_i
    rows = np.zeros((w.shape[1], nb * nl), np.float32)
    conv = np.zeros_like(rows)
    np.add.at(rows, (idx, cell), 1)
    np.add.at(conv, (idx, cell), df["converted"].to_numpy())

    def ratio(r, c):
        r, c = r.reshape(*r.shape[:-1], nb, nl), c.reshape(*c.shape[:-1], nb, nl)
        band_rate = c.sum(-1, keepdims=True) / np.maximum(r.sum(-1, keepdims=True), 1)
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            return c.sum(-2) / (r * band_rate).sum(-2), (r * band_rate).sum(-2)

    est, expected = ratio(rows.sum(0), conv.sum(0))
    draws = np.vstack([ratio(w[s:s + 100] @ rows, w[s:s + 100] @ conv)[0] for s in range(0, len(w), 100)])
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):
        lo, hi = np.nanquantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975], axis=0)
    return est, lo, hi, expected

def signal_table(feat, specs=signal_specs):
    # one row per feature level, for all eligible donors and for never-major donors
    idx, w = couple_draws(feat)
    never = ~feat["former_major"].to_numpy()
    base = feat["converted"].mean()
    out = []
    for name, expr, levels in specs:
        d = feat.with_columns(level=expr)
        est, lo, hi, expected = within_band_ratio(d, idx, w, levels)
        n_est, n_lo, n_hi, _ = within_band_ratio(d.filter(~pl.col("former_major")), idx[never], w, levels)
        counts = {r["level"]: r for r in d.group_by("level").agg(n=pl.len(), c=pl.col("converted").sum()).iter_rows(named=True)}
        for i, lev in enumerate(levels):
            n_rows, n_conv = counts[lev]["n"], counts[lev]["c"]
            out.append({"feature": name, "level": lev, "donor_years": n_rows, "converters": n_conv,
                        "rate": n_conv / n_rows, "lift": n_conv / n_rows / base, "expected": expected[i],
                        "ratio": est[i], "ci_low": lo[i], "ci_high": hi[i],
                        "never_ratio": None if name == "Former major donor" else n_est[i],
                        "never_low": None if name == "Former major donor" else n_lo[i],
                        "never_high": None if name == "Former major donor" else n_hi[i]})
    return pl.DataFrame(out)

def ratio_text(r, lo, hi, conv):
    if r is None:
        return "not applicable"
    return "no converters" if conv == 0 else f"{r:.2f} ({lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f})"

def display_signals(tbl):
    return tbl.with_columns(
        pl.col("lift").round(2), pl.col("expected").round(1),
        within_band_ratio=pl.struct("ratio", "ci_low", "ci_high", "converters").map_elements(
            lambda s: ratio_text(s["ratio"], s["ci_low"], s["ci_high"], s["converters"]), return_dtype=pl.String),
        never_major_ratio=pl.struct("never_ratio", "never_low", "never_high", "converters").map_elements(
            lambda s: ratio_text(s["never_ratio"], s["never_low"], s["never_high"], s["converters"]), return_dtype=pl.String),
    ).select("feature", "level", "donor_years", "converters", "rate", "lift", "expected", "within_band_ratio", "never_major_ratio")

signals12 = signal_table(feat12)

def sig(feature, level, col="ratio", tbl=signals12):
    return tbl.filter((pl.col("feature") == feature) & (pl.col("level") == level))[col][0]

def ci(feature, level, never=False, tbl=signals12):
    # a ratio with its interval, for the text
    cols = ("never_ratio", "never_low", "never_high") if never else ("ratio", "ci_low", "ci_high")
    r, lo, hi = (sig(feature, level, c, tbl) for c in cols)
    return f"{r:.2f} ({lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f})"

# share of converters at a level who are former major donors
def former_share(expr):
    return feat12.filter(expr & pl.col("converted"))["former_major"].mean()

former_gave_less = former_share(pl.col("prior_total") < pl.col("prev_total"))
former_two_years = former_share(pl.col("two_years_before") >= 1200)
former_soft_before = former_share(pl.col("soft_before"))

# where upgrade and soft-credit donors sit in prior-year giving
upgrade_top = (feat12.filter("upgrade_gift")["prior_total"] > 240).mean()
soft_t_top = (feat12.filter("soft_in_t")["prior_total"] > 240).mean()
all_top = (feat12["prior_total"] > 240).mean()

show(display_signals(signals12), pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Giving-history signals: overall lift and ratio within prior-year bands, 12 month outcome")
plot_df = pl.concat([
    signals12.select("feature", "level", "ratio", "ci_low", "ci_high", "converters", group=pl.lit("All eligible")),
    signals12.select("feature", "level", ratio="never_ratio", ci_low="never_low", ci_high="never_high",
                     converters="converters", group=pl.lit("Never major")),
]).filter((pl.col("converters") > 0) & pl.col("ratio").is_not_null()).with_columns(
    # escape dollar signs so matplotlib does not read them as math
    label=(pl.col("feature") + ": " + pl.col("level")).str.replace_all("$", r"\$", literal=True)
)
label_order = list(dict.fromkeys(plot_df["label"].to_list()))[::-1]
plot_pd = plot_df.to_pandas()
plot_pd["label"] = plot_pd["label"].astype("category").cat.set_categories(label_order)

(
    ggplot(plot_pd, aes("label", "ratio", color="group"))
    + geom_hline(yintercept=1, linetype="dashed", color="grey")
    + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin="ci_low", ymax="ci_high"), position=position_dodge(width=0.6), size=0.3)
    + scale_y_log10()
    + coord_flip()
    + labs(x="", y="Observed over expected converters (log scale)", color="",
           title="Signal beyond prior-year giving",
           subtitle="12 month outcome, FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts, 95% intervals")
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 11), legend_position="top")
)

Most features with large overall lift add much less once prior-year giving is held constant:

  • Former major status is one of the largest added signals. Former major donors convert at 3.18 (2.70 to 3.82) times the rate their prior-year giving predicts. Only giving less than the year before is higher, and those converters are mostly former major donors as well (below).
  • Short giving histories are the clearest negative signal. Donors in their first year of giving, donors who gave in only one of the last five years, and donors with no gift the year before convert at about a fifth of the expected rate (0.20, 0.20, and 0.22). This holds for never-major donors (0.34, 0.35, and 0.37). The gain at the other end is smaller: giving in all five years is 1.54 (1.40 to 1.69) overall and 1.34 (1.05 to 1.63) for never-major donors.
  • Legacy history helps. Donors with no legacy-era gifts convert at 0.35 (0.19 to 0.54) times the expected rate, and 0.56 (0.31 to 0.84) among never-major donors. This supports keeping Erin’s legacy history indicators alongside the legacy amounts.
  • Some signals mostly mark former major donors. Giving less than the year before, $1,200 or more in the two years before, and a soft credit before FY t have ratios of 3.28 (2.64 to 3.95), 2.61 (2.24 to 3.02), and 2.08 (1.76 to 2.44). Among never-major donors they fall to 0.81 (0.18 to 1.66), 1.81 (0.73 to 2.97), and 1.57 (0.90 to 2.36), with intervals that include 1. The converters at these levels are mostly former major donors stepping down from a major year (93%, 92%, and 82%).
  • Upgrade gifts and soft credits in FY t add nothing. An upgrade gift has an overall lift of 8.5 and a soft credit in FY t 20.2, and Benjamin’s and Kate’s EDAs listed both as strong signals on that basis. Within bands the ratios are 0.55 (0.40 to 0.72) and 1.05 (0.87 to 1.22), and for never-major donors 1.03 (0.75 to 1.31) and 0.91 (0.61 to 1.25). Their overall lift comes from where these donors sit: all upgrade-gift donor-years and 59% of soft-credit donor-years gave more than $240 in FY t, compared with 6.8% of all eligible donor-years.
  • How the year’s giving was made matters a little. Donors who gave the year’s whole amount in one gift convert at 1.45 (1.16 to 1.74) times the expected rate (1.49 (1.07 to 1.95) for never-major donors). Additional gifts point the other way, at 0.61 (0.35 to 0.86) among never-major donors.
  • Sustainers convert somewhat less than their giving predicts. Sustainers giving $10 a month or less are at 0.79 (0.65 to 0.96), and none of the 2,227 donor-years giving more than $25 a month converted, where about 8 were expected.

Recency and Sustainer Status

Overall, recency looks like a strong signal: donors whose last gift came within 30 days of year end have a lift of 2.8, while the 31 to 90 day group has a lift of 0.34. Within bands the order changes: the most recent group falls to 0.88, and donors whose last gift was more than 180 days before year end are highest at 1.51. Monthly sustainers drive much of the overall pattern, so the table splits recency by sustainer status.

sust_recency = feat12.with_columns(
    level=pl.when(pl.col("sustainer"))
        .then(pl.lit("sustainer, ") + pl.col("days_since_last_gift").cut([30, 90], labels=["30 or less", "31 to 90", "over 90"]).cast(pl.String))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("not a sustainer, ") + pl.col("days_since_last_gift").cut([30, 90, 180], labels=["30 or less", "31 to 90", "91 to 180", "over 180"]).cast(pl.String))
)
rs_levels = ["sustainer, 30 or less", "sustainer, 31 to 90", "sustainer, over 90",
             "not a sustainer, 30 or less", "not a sustainer, 31 to 90", "not a sustainer, 91 to 180", "not a sustainer, over 180"]
rs_idx, rs_w = couple_draws(sust_recency)
rs_est, rs_lo, rs_hi, rs_exp = within_band_ratio(sust_recency, rs_idx, rs_w, rs_levels)
rs_counts = {r["level"]: r for r in sust_recency.group_by("level").agg(n=pl.len(), c=pl.col("converted").sum()).iter_rows(named=True)}
recency_sustainer = pl.DataFrame([
    {"group": lev, "donor_years": rs_counts[lev]["n"], "converters": rs_counts[lev]["c"],
     "rate": rs_counts[lev]["c"] / rs_counts[lev]["n"], "expected": round(float(rs_exp[i]), 1),
     "within_band_ratio": ratio_text(rs_est[i], rs_lo[i], rs_hi[i], rs_counts[lev]["c"])}
    for i, lev in enumerate(rs_levels)
])
rs = {r["group"]: r for r in recency_sustainer.iter_rows(named=True)}
sust_share_31_90 = feat12.filter(pl.col("days_since_last_gift").is_between(31, 90))["sustainer"].mean()

# share of sustainers above $240 in FY t, by recency
sust = feat12.filter("sustainer")
sust_top_recent = (sust.filter(pl.col("days_since_last_gift") <= 30)["prior_total"] > 240).mean()
sust_top_31_90 = (sust.filter(pl.col("days_since_last_gift").is_between(31, 90))["prior_total"] > 240).mean()

show(recency_sustainer, pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Recency split by sustainer status, within prior-year bands")

Sustainers make up 87.6% of the 31 to 90 day group. In raw rates, sustainers with a gift in the last 30 days convert at 0.40% and those whose last gift was 31 to 90 days before year end at 0.024%. That gap comes from prior-year giving, not recency: 28% of the recent sustainers gave more than $240 in FY t, compared with 0.9% of the others. Within bands both groups convert below their expected rate (0.77 (0.63 to 0.91) and 0.80 (0.50 to 1.08)). Among donors who are not sustainers, the most recent and least recent groups are both above expected (1.56 (1.02 to 2.10) and 1.56 (1.19 to 1.92)) and the middle groups are near 1, so there is no steady trend. Sustainer status carries more information than recency, and recency should not be scored as a straight line. This matters for the recency, frequency, and value baseline in the baselines section.

Longer Window Check

The same comparison for the 3 year outcome uses the FY2021 and FY2022 cohorts, the only ones whose 3 year windows end before FY2026.

NoteSignals within giving bands, 3 year outcome 
signals3 = signal_table(feat3)
show(display_signals(signals3), pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Giving-history signals within prior-year bands, 3 year outcome")
# levels with at least 10 converters at 12 months, and whether the 3 year ratio falls on the same side of 1
both = signals12.join(signals3.select("feature", "level", ratio3="ratio", conv3="converters"), on=["feature", "level"]).filter(
    (pl.col("converters") >= 10) & (pl.col("conv3") >= 10)
)
same_side = ((both["ratio"] > 1) == (both["ratio3"] > 1)).mean()
flipped = both.filter((pl.col("ratio") > 1) != (pl.col("ratio3") > 1))
flipped_low = flipped.select(pl.min_horizontal("ratio", "ratio3")).to_series().min()
flipped_high = flipped.select(pl.max_horizontal("ratio", "ratio3")).to_series().max()

The 3 year results follow the 12 month results closely: for the 39 levels with at least 10 converters in both windows, 87% of the ratios fall on the same side of 1. The 5 levels that switch sides all have ratios between 0.73 and 1.14 in both windows, so none of them changes from a clear signal to its opposite. Former major status and short giving histories remain the strongest signals at 3 years.

Summary for Modeling

  • Prior-year giving carries most of the signal. The other features should be judged by what they add to it, and most add much less than their overall lift suggests.
  • The features that add signal are former major status, giving history length (years given in the last five, years since first gift, legacy-era years, a gift the year before), whether the year’s giving came in one gift, and sustainer status. Recency adds little once prior-year giving and sustainer status are known.
  • Upgrade gifts and soft credits in FY t can stay in the feature set, but they should not be described to staff as signs of major potential.
  • Among never-major donors, the added signal is mostly about history length and the shape of the year’s giving, so the model will rely heavily on prior-year giving for this group.

Solicitation and Passport Viewing

The individual EDAs disagreed on whether solicitation and Passport viewing help predict conversion. Erin’s and Samantha’s EDAs compared overall rates, while Benjamin’s and Kate’s compared rates within bands of prior-year giving. This section applies the within-band test from the previous section (decision 7) to both, using the same validation cohorts, the 12 month outcome, and the same five bands. Both sources only begin in FY2021, so they cannot be used for cohorts before then.

Solicitation Volume and Timing

sol = bp.solicitation_by_year(clean)
cm_dates = clean["campaign_members"]
start_marker = cm_dates["campaign_start_date"].dt.strftime("%m-%d").unique().to_list()
responses = cm_dates.filter("responded").with_columns(
    campaign_fy=bp.fiscal_year("campaign_start_date"), response_fy=bp.fiscal_year("responded_date"))
response_same_fy = (responses["campaign_fy"] == responses["response_fy"]).mean()
response_types = responses["response_type"].unique().to_list()

donors_fy = person_years.select("constituent_id", "fy")
sol_volume = (
    sol.join(donors_fy, on=["constituent_id", "fy"], how="semi")
    .group_by("fy")
    .agg(donors_solicited=pl.len(), solicitations=pl.col("solicitations").sum(), responses=pl.col("responses").sum())
    .join(donors_fy.group_by("fy").agg(donors=pl.len()), on="fy")
    .with_columns(share_of_donors_solicited=pl.col("donors_solicited") / pl.col("donors"),
                  solicitations_per_donor=(pl.col("solicitations") / pl.col("donors_solicited")).round(1),
                  response_rate=pl.col("responses") / pl.col("solicitations"))
    .select("fy", "donors", "share_of_donors_solicited", "solicitations_per_donor", "response_rate")
    .sort("fy")
)
sv = {r["fy"]: r for r in sol_volume.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(sol_volume, pct_cols=["share_of_donors_solicited", "response_rate"], caption="Share of donors solicited and response rate by fiscal year")

Every campaign start date is 07/01, so it marks the fiscal year and not the date of the ask. A response is a payment on that marketing code (the only response type is Payment). Following Samantha’s rule, a response counts in the fiscal year of its response date, since that is when it becomes known. In this data every response falls in the same fiscal year as its campaign, so the rule gives the same counts as using the campaign year, and every response used for a FY t snapshot is known by June 30 of FY t.

The share of donors solicited rose from 74.7% in FY2021 to 89.6% in FY2022 and nearly all donors from FY2023 on, while solicitations per solicited donor stayed close to 15. That change reflects PBS Utah’s mailing decisions, not donor behavior, so whether a donor was solicited depends partly on the year.

Solicitation Within Giving Bands

Solicitation features are counted for FY t: number of solicitations, responses, and whether any solicitation came by mail, email, digital, or phone and in person combined (both are rare). The three-year count follows Erin’s EDA and covers FY t-2 to FY t. Because solicitation records start in FY2021, the FY2021 and FY2022 cohorts have only one and two years of it.

feat_sol = feat12.join(bp.solicitation_features(feat12, sol), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
share_solicited = (feat_sol["solicitations"] > 0).mean()
unsolicited_cohorts = sorted(feat_sol.filter(pl.col("solicitations") == 0)["t"].unique().to_list())

sol_specs = [
    ("Solicitations in FY t", pl.col("solicitations").cut([0, 1, 10, 30], labels=["none", "1", "2 to 10", "11 to 30", "over 30"]).cast(pl.String),
     ["none", "1", "2 to 10", "11 to 30", "over 30"]),
    ("Solicitations, FY t-2 to FY t", pl.col("solicitations_3yr").cut([0, 5, 20, 60], labels=["none", "1 to 5", "6 to 20", "21 to 60", "over 60"]).cast(pl.String),
     ["none", "1 to 5", "6 to 20", "21 to 60", "over 60"]),
    ("Responses in FY t", pl.col("responses").cut([0, 1], labels=["none", "1", "2 or more"]).cast(pl.String), ["none", "1", "2 or more"]),
    ("Mail solicitation in FY t", yes_no("by_mail"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Email solicitation in FY t", yes_no("by_email"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Digital solicitation in FY t", yes_no("by_digital"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Phone or in-person solicitation in FY t", yes_no("by_phone_or_in_person"), ["no", "yes"]),
]
sol_signals = signal_table(feat_sol, sol_specs)

def ssig(feature, level, col="ratio"):
    return sig(feature, level, col, tbl=sol_signals)

def sci(feature, level, never=False):
    return ci(feature, level, never, tbl=sol_signals)

show(display_signals(sol_signals), pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Solicitation features within prior-year bands, 12 month outcome")

91.4% of eligible donors were solicited at least once in FY t, and every unsolicited donor-year comes from the FY2021 and FY2022 cohorts, before solicitation reached nearly everyone. Once prior-year giving is held constant, solicitation adds little:

  • Volume. No volume group converts clearly more or less often than its giving predicts, and most intervals include 1. The highest volume groups are 1.05 (0.63 to 1.47) in FY t and 1.21 (0.78 to 1.70) over three years.
  • Responses. Donors with one response have an overall lift of 1.22 but a within-band ratio of 0.98 (0.80 to 1.18). A response is a payment that is already part of prior-year giving, so it carries little new information.
  • Channels. No channel stands out. Phone or in-person solicitation, which might mark donors staff already see as prospects, reaches 4,238 donor-years and only 7 converters, a ratio of 1.16 (0.38 to 2.14).

Solicitations in the Outcome Year

next_sol = sol.select("constituent_id", t=pl.col("fy") - 1, outcome_year=pl.col("solicitations"))
outcome_sol = (
    feat_sol.join(next_sol, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    .with_columns(pl.col("outcome_year").fill_null(0), top_band=pl.col("band") == "over $500")
    .group_by("top_band", "converted")
    .agg(donor_years=pl.len(), solicitations_fy_t=pl.col("solicitations").mean(), solicitations_outcome_year=pl.col("outcome_year").mean())
    .with_columns(pl.col("solicitations_fy_t", "solicitations_outcome_year").round(1),
                  group=pl.when(pl.col("top_band")).then(pl.lit("gave over $500 in FY t")).otherwise(pl.lit("gave $500 or less")))
    .select("group", "converted", "donor_years", "solicitations_fy_t", "solicitations_outcome_year")
    .sort("group", "converted")
)
osol = {(r["group"], r["converted"]): r for r in outcome_sol.iter_rows(named=True)}
top = "gave over $500 in FY t"
show(outcome_sol, caption="Average solicitations in FY t and in the outcome year, converters compared with others")

Among donors who gave over $500 in FY t, converters and non-converters received a similar number of solicitations in FY t (12.2 and 12.7 on average). In the outcome year, converters received 6.4 and non-converters 11.7. The data does not say why, but outcome-year solicitations move with the outcome and must not be used as features. Outcome-year responses are payments in the outcome year and are excluded for the same reason.

Passport Coverage

The Passport table records titles viewed and the average share of each title watched, by person, fiscal year, and genre. A person-year only appears if something was watched, so a missing year can mean no linked account, no consent to share viewing, or no viewing. Following Erin’s EDA, a missing year is kept as its own “no viewing record” level instead of being treated as zero viewing.

pv = clean["passport"]
viewer_years = pv.select("constituent_id", fy=pl.col("fiscal_year")).unique()

def again_next_year(df, fy):
    this_year = df.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy)
    return this_year.join(df.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy + 1), on="constituent_id", how="semi").height / this_year.height

passport_cov = pl.DataFrame([
    {"fy": fy, "viewers": viewer_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy).height,
     "share_who_gave": viewer_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy).join(donors_fy, on=["constituent_id", "fy"], how="semi").height
                       / viewer_years.filter(pl.col("fy") == fy).height,
     "viewers_again_next_year": again_next_year(viewer_years, fy), "donors_again_next_year": again_next_year(donors_fy, fy)}
    for fy in range(2021, 2026)
])
view_again = passport_cov["viewers_again_next_year"]
give_again = passport_cov["donors_again_next_year"]
show(passport_cov, pct_cols=["share_who_gave", "viewers_again_next_year", "donors_again_next_year"], caption="Passport viewers by year and how often viewing carries over")

Most viewers gave in the same year, which fits Passport being a member benefit. Viewing carries over from year to year much less than giving does: 34% to 41% of a year’s viewers have a record the next year, compared with 75% to 80% of donors who give again. This affects how viewing features behave, because a donor’s viewing record in FY t says little about the next year, so the analysis includes both a FY t flag and a flag for any viewing record through FY t.

Passport Within Giving Bands

feat_pv = feat12.join(bp.passport_features(feat12, pv), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
share_viewed_t = feat_pv["viewed_t"].mean()
rho_titles_prior = feat_pv.filter("viewed_t").select(pl.corr("titles", "prior_total", method="spearman")).item()

NO_RECORD = "no viewing record"
def viewing_level(expr, cuts, labels):
    return pl.when(~pl.col("viewed_t")).then(pl.lit(NO_RECORD)).otherwise(expr.cut(cuts, labels=labels).cast(pl.String))

pv_specs = [
    ("Viewing record in FY t", yes_no("viewed_t"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Viewing record through FY t", yes_no("viewed_by_t"), ["no", "yes"]),
    ("Titles viewed in FY t", viewing_level(pl.col("titles"), [15, 40], ["1 to 15", "16 to 40", "over 40"]),
     [NO_RECORD, "1 to 15", "16 to 40", "over 40"]),
    ("Genres viewed in FY t", viewing_level(pl.col("genres"), [2, 4], ["1 to 2", "3 to 4", "5 or more"]),
     [NO_RECORD, "1 to 2", "3 to 4", "5 or more"]),
    ("Share of titles watched", viewing_level(pl.col("share_watched"), [0.6, 0.85], ["under 60%", "60% to 85%", "over 85%"]),
     [NO_RECORD, "under 60%", "60% to 85%", "over 85%"]),
]
pv_signals = signal_table(feat_pv, pv_specs)

def psig(feature, level, col="ratio"):
    return sig(feature, level, col, tbl=pv_signals)

def pci(feature, level, never=False):
    return ci(feature, level, never, tbl=pv_signals)

# titles viewed, observed over expected in each cohort and at 3 years (band rates from the pooled cohorts)
def titles_by(feat, by):
    return (
        feat.with_columns(level=pv_specs[2][1], band_rate=pl.col("converted").mean().over("band"))
        .group_by(by).agg(observed=pl.col("converted").sum(), expected=pl.col("band_rate").sum())
        .with_columns(ratio=pl.col("observed") / pl.col("expected"))
    )

titles_cohort = titles_by(feat_pv, ["t", "level"])
heavy_by_cohort = titles_cohort.filter(pl.col("level") == "over 40")
light_by_cohort = titles_cohort.filter(pl.col("level") == "1 to 15")
feat_pv3 = feat3.join(bp.passport_features(feat3, pv), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
titles3 = {r["level"]: r["ratio"] for r in titles_by(feat_pv3, ["level"]).iter_rows(named=True)}

show(display_signals(pv_signals), pct_cols=["rate"], pct_digits=3, caption="Passport features within prior-year bands, 12 month outcome")

50.3% of eligible donors have a viewing record in FY t, and among them the rank correlation between titles viewed and prior-year giving is 0.01, so viewing and giving are nearly unrelated. Having a viewing record adds nothing: viewers have an overall lift of 0.72 and a within-band ratio of 1.08 (0.88 to 1.29). Completion and genre breadth add little as well, with intervals that include 1 at every level.

The number of titles viewed is the exception.
